div.p: FROM WARRINGTON TO THE LAND'S END-AND BACK. No. 111.
TUE LAND'S END.

revelries is the most westerly town in England, and is of acme importance. It contains about 11,000 in- habitants, but it must not be compared to a Lancashire own of the same size. It has numbers of large hotels, ree3ly fine public buildings, and an esplanade quit° equal to that of Ryde. Then, it has the advantage of a beautiful situation. Built on a declivity, girt by hills on the North and East, with Mount's Bay, and St. Michael's in the distance, it is truly the "Fair citY of the West." We spent a quiet day in examining the town and immediate neighbourhood, and what astonished us most of all, was the enormous size, abundance and beauty of the geraniums which adorned the cottage gardens, some certainly were 16 feet high covering almost the whole of the front of the house. The history of the town is interesting, but I will not trouble you with it, you can get it all from Murray or Black. Let this be enough; it is the birthplace of Sir Humphrey Davy whose statue stands in front of the Post Office ;it was sacked by the Spaniards. ravaged by the Roundheads under Fairfax, and visited by Queen Victoria. Our loyal panty trod in her steps, for we placed our " leVaukenphast" on the dainty little copper sole which marks the place where her Majesty landed at St. Michael's Mount. The visit to it. Michael's is a delightful one. There ja no English, perhaps, so well known as this. Photo- graphs, paintings, scenes in plays and even woodcuts In school histories delight in picturing "The guarded Mount" as Milton calls it. It is a stupendous peak of greenstone standing out boldly in the middle of the broad bay. The old coachman, as the scene lay before us descanted rapturously on its beauties. "I've seen that view, sir, every day for the last forty years, and I never pass it without thinking it the finest place in the world." He certainly had heard of the Bay of Naples and other noted spots; but, with the confidence of Ignorance he was quite sure no place on earth could come up to this, and he was rather annoyed that any One should suggest such a thing. And, certainly, at all finesse the castellated mountain forms a beautiful object, its dark mass standing out boldly in the bright- MU of noon-day, and at sunset seeming to attract round its head all the glorious colours of the surround- ing sky. We vieited it from Marazion, an old Jewish colcny, called also Market Jew, at cne time the com- mercial rival of Penzance. At low water there is a natural causeway 1,200 yards long, connectieg the Mount and the main land. The mountain has always had a sacred character. St. Michael, of course, paid visits to the spot, to see an anchorite who dwelt there, so it is said. St. Ksyin visited it from Ireland in the Bth century; it was a Bene- dictine monastery before the Conquest; it disputes with the Isle of Wight the honour of being the leas of Diodorua Siculus, where the Britons brought their tin to trade with the Phenicians. It has been a place of refuge at all times. Here it was that the Fair Rose of Scotland, Katherine Gordon, took refuge after the failure of her husband, Warbeck. During the religious disturbances of Henry the Eighth's reign it was cap. hired by some peasants, who climbed up behind trusses of hay. It was taken and retaken dining the civil wars of the 17th century. Now, it is occupied by the Bt. Aubin family, who are doing all that Art can do to perfect what Nature has done so well. Such is, very briefly, the history of this glorious place ; but far more interesting to us were the beautiful panoramas we got from the different points of view, and, must we confess it, we preferred watchiag the gambols of some Sunday School children, who had come for a pic- nic, and were disporting themselves on the mountain aides. At last we are in the coach which takes us to Land's End, we see our goal before us. In point of beauty, we are told, it does not equal the Lizard; but to see it was a matter of moral compulsion. To be a; Penzance and not see the Land's End I As well go to Winwick and not visit the church, 85 well visit Liverpool with- out seeing St. George's Hall. SJ we entered the well- appointed covered car which runs daily in the summer months, starting at eleven, returning about fire, giv- ing one hour at the Logan Rock, and two at the Land's End, going by Buryan and returning by Sennen. St. Buryan has nothing striking about it except its per- pendicular church, whose lofty tower serves as a land- mark to the whole district. Treryn Castle is a grand rocky promontory, about twenty minutes' walk from the rude hamlet of Treryn. The old man who acted as cur guide oid his best to make us see the remains of a tiiple valley and fosse, but he hardly succeeded, we were more interested in the famous Logan Rock. There are many of these" rockiug stones" in the county, and some persons have thought they are Druidical in character. But this feeling has often foand expression among our cousins of the West. "With cliffs of white and bowers of green, And ocean narrowing to caress her, And hills and threat:led streams between, Our little mother isle, God bless her " On our return we passed through Sennen, and paid A visit to the .dYinetcen Merry Maidens. As Lancashire men we hold to the fame of Lancashire witches. Corn- wall has many fair daughters; were these of the num- ber ? We found they were nineteen long blocks of 1 stone irregularly scattered over a field. What a satire Who gave them the name P Was it some disappointed bachelor, who likened merry maidens to these stead- fast blocks of granite? Or did some happy benedict fio style this ancient and grim circle of Druidical stones As a warning to old maids. Who can tell? Musing on these things we arrive at Penzance.

THE INQUEST.

Considerable excitement and regret was oceesioned in Warrington on Saturday morning last, through a report that Mr. John Morin, who for 20 years has been in-the employ of the Warrington Waterworks Company, at clerk,. had committed suicide by catting _ _ his throat. On inquiry, however, it was found that the extent of the injuries were not so great as had been reported, and the medical men in attendance an- ticipated his recovery. He progressed favourably until Monday night, when about half-past eight he was frightened by a very loud report of a cannon which some thoughtless youths had fired from under the rail way arch adjacent to Mr. Plevin's house in Allen- street. The shock to the system was so great that he died in an hour afterwards. Some reckless and pre- cipitate correspondent had announeed in a Liverpool paper deceased's death a day before it took place, an announcement which naturally gave great pain and offence to the deceased's friends and relatives. It is however just to state that the next day, acting upon authentic information, the newspaper in question con- tradicted the statement which had been supplied to it in such heartless and indecent haste. Mr. Pleviu was secretary for various building and friendly societies in the town, notably for the Olive Branch Lodge of the Order of Oddfellows, and in that capacity he wz s widely known and respected. The inquest was held on Thursday morning at the Ram's Head Hotel, before Mr. C. E. Driffield. Mr. Nicholson (of the firm of Nicholson, White, and Nicholson) attended on behalf of the Warrington Waterworks Company, at the request of the directors. Mr. Bowes, master of the Blue Coat School, also at- tended, the deceased having been formerly connected with the school as a day scholar. The evidence called showed that on the morning in question after Mrs. Plevin had left the bedroom, her husband jumped out of bed, went into the other room, and seizing a razor, cut his throat. Alarm was given, and Dr. Spinks and Dr. Starkey Smith promptly attended, and did all that was possible under the circumstances. When Dr. Spanks asked him what had led him to commit the rash act, he replied," Mad, mad." He had seen him on the Friday previous, when he seemed all right. When he went to him on the Saturday morning he found strong symptoms of insanity, and he was very violent. Mr. Fogg, relieving officer, said he saw the deceased on the Friday night, and was with him for a consider- able time. On Friday morning Mrs. Plevin had told him that her husband had,bad a nervous fit, and in the evening he saw him, and tried teraise his spirits. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE WARRINGTON ORANGEMEN. Monday evening last was distinguished in War- rington by the celebration of the anniversary of the various Orange lodges in the town, presided over by Bro. Councillor Kean. The occasion was marked by a tea party and ball, which was attended by about CO ladies and gentlemen. The brethren on the platform, which included Bro. Galloway, Bro. Bloomfield, Bro. Ford, Bro. Lees, and other gentlemen, were gaily or- namented with ribbons, sashes, and favours, the pris- matic combination of which reminded the observer of Joseph's coat of many colours. Banners and flags, bearing the name of the "Immortal William," who is said to have saved the English fromr"bress money and wooden shoes," were suspended from the walla of the hall, and these, together with the striking colours worn by the ladies, imparted animation to the vene. After tea, which was provided in Mr. and Mrs. Pot. ter's best style, becoming the importance of the occa- sion, the Chairman delivered his opening address, and was followed by Bro. Galloway and other prominent officials of the order. The speech of the evening, how- ever, was delivered by a certain Bro. Ford, who is the treasurer of lodge 162. Selecting the Ex-Prime ' Minister for his theme, the orator in an energetic and trenchant style, delivered himself as fellows, the report which we present to our readers being a faithful and verbatim account of his oration The man that caused me to become an Orangeman was William Gladstone. (Slight applause.) It was through his disestablishing and disendowing the Irian Church. "William" Gladstone is anxious to see his name in print. (Hear, hear.) When he has nothing else to do he will go and cut a oak tree down, and get some friend to stand near and ilea him do it, so that it will get in the papers. (Hear, hear.) He is as much use to the English nation as he is for cutting oak trees down, but it would have been a great deal better for the country if he had been asleep in his arm chair for the lest az months. (Cheers.) Look what he's been doing, if it had not been for him and the friends coming forward as they have done, agitating the minds of the people, and causing Rowe& to think that the Engliih people were siding with them, there would not have been one-thousandth part of the blood shed in Baguia as there has been." Tremendous cheering followed the speech, after which the company amused themselves, led by an irrepressible Smi of Mars, by firing off 21 guns, to the honour of two distinguished gentlemen, the Chairman and the Earl of Enniskillen. The oratorical portion of the programme was brought to a close by the uairman vigorously calling for three cheers for the Queen and Emprers of India, which were as vigorously responded to. Dancing followed terminating in the small hours of the following morn- ing.

div.head: HABITUAL DETENTKARD'S BILL.
div.p: THE HABITUAL DETENTKARD'S BILL.

A London correspondent says that under the direc- tion of Mrs. Dalrymple, widow of Dr. Dalrymple, M.P., a committee has been formed for the purpose of dealing with the question of habitual drunkards, and arrangements havwbeen madw to bring in a bill next session. The committee includes Lord Shaftesbary, who is its chairman, the Archbishop of Canterbnry, several bishops, and a number of M.P.'s. The bill will be supported, it is said, by the full strength of the medical profession.

CORN GROWING LOSSES IN ENGLAND. Mr. Read, M.P., speaking on Saturday, at the Northwich Chamber of Agriculture, on agricultural topics, said corn growing did not pay in this country. The cultivation of wheat this year had been a dead loss to the farmers. Thousands of acres that would not realise £8 an acre had cost Ll for ingathering. The same price was paid in Norfolk for light or heavy crops, while the work was often disgracefully done. He advocated paying for havesting by the acre, com- mencing harvesting earlier, and so utilise favourable weather and prepare for autumn cultivation.

div.head: UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE.
div.p: THE UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE.

Nearly 3,000 persons attended a United Kingdom Alliance meeting in Bristol, on Tuesday night, to hear speeches from; amongst others, Sir Wilfrid Lawson and Mr. Morley, M.P. Sir Wilfrid made an earnest and amusingspeecti, in which he referred to the many efforts of drinking reform that had been made, es- pecially by the Beer Act and the cheap wines measure of Mr. Gladstone, and said the last state of the country was worse than the first.—Mr. Morley announced hims Elf as a convert to the principles of the Permissive Bill, an announcement which provoked considerable applause.

On Saturday, at the Newton-le-Willows Fatty Sessions, Edward Johnson, owner of the Golhorne Sinking Pits, and James Sharpies, manager, were charged under the Coal Mines Regulation, 1872, with not having the tops of two working shafts properly fenced; secondly, with not causing an abstract of the Act to be posted at the mine; and, thirdly, with not having attached to the machine for lowering or raising pers ma into or from the mines a proper indicator. Mr. Gregory, of Liverpool, prosecuted, and Mr. Ap- pleton, of Wigan, appeared for the defendants and pleaded guilty to the charges. He said prior to the hit of the inspector (Mr. Hedley) the shafts were fenced, but the fencing had been removed to put down an engine, and had not been replaced as it ought to 'have been. The same explanation applied to the second charge; and with regard to the third charge, he said before the inspector visited the-place there was a mark on the rope, but the indicator had not been put; up through the changes that were being effected.l The Bench, Colonel McCorquodale presiding, fined the owner three guineas in each_ case, and the manager 1 one guinea in each case.

• The World states that the Bishop of Sodor and Man, the hon. and Right Rev. Horatio Powys, is about to resign his see on account of ill-health. His lordship has decided on this course, it is to be imagined, in con- sequence of the continuous grumbling of the Manx. men for the last two years at the Bishop's dislike to their country. Dr. Powys, it is said, has not visited his diocese for some twenty-two months or so, so the Mammon have certainly a prima facie excuse for dis- satisfaction. They, by the by, are canny folk in their way, and in order to secure the residence on their is- land of the next appointed prelate they are making the cunning proposal to reduce the episcopal stipend by nearly one half —namely, from £2,000 to £1,200 per annum, and divide the surplus among the insular clergy. Whether or not the straitening of the bishop's income will serve to confine him for economy's sake to a place where herrings and eau de cologne are cheap remains bbe proved. Dr. Powys, it may be added, is a son of the late Lord Lilford, and as Bishop of Sodor and Man possesses (and this is a lid not generally known) a seat in the House of Lords, though he may neither vote nor interfere in the proceedings thereof.— Liverpool Daily _Post.

THE REGISTRAR GENERAL'S REPORT. The Registrar General's quarterly return of births, deaths, and marriages has just been issued, from which it appears that in the united kingdom the births of 280,083 children, and 154,858 deaths were registered. The natural increase was thus 125,225. During the June quarter 102,436 persons were married, and this was equal to an annual rate of 16.9 per 1,000 in England and Wales. The births in England and Wales in last September quarter were 216,167, yielding an annual rate for the quarter of 35.4 per 1,000. There were 119,909 deaths giving a rate of 19.6. They included 62,560 of males, and 57,349 -of females. The lowest death rate in Counties was in Westmoreland 14.7, the highest being in Lancaster 23.5, and Leicester 23.9.

Of the total emigrants last quarter 22,455 were English, 3,405 Scotch, and 7,007 Irish. BILLIARDS AT WARRINGTON. COOK V. TIMBRELL.

Mr. W. D. Brazendale, the new proprietor of the Patten Arms Hotel, opened his well-appointed billiard room on Saturday evening, the occasion being die. tinguished by the presence of the renowned billiard champion of England, Mr. Cook, who had undertaken a match against Mr. Timbrelll, the Liverpool cham- pion, giving him 300 points in a game of 1,000 up. Owing to the anpunetuality of the trains the players ware an hour behind time, and many gentlemen, who had come down from Manchester, Widnes, and the adjoining neighbourhood to witness the match, fearing that Mr. Cook would not put in an appearance, re- turned home by the next train. However, a fair had select audience remained, and when Mr. Cook and his opponent did arrive their reception was of a most cordial character. Cook commenced the game by giving a miss in baulk, and Timbrell followed him with a good all round break of 75, hi i second break reaching 27, the former elicit- ing warm applause, and, in fact, was his break of the evening. Cook'. first break was one of 19, whilla was followed by an all round break of 38, and another break of 49. It was evident that Cook was in good form, the precision and steadiness with which he handled his cue calling forth the admiration of the spectators. Tirabrell however, did not appear to be in good form, his hurried journey having somewhat un- settled him. In fact, he did not suceeed in doing anything remarkable in the intervening play. The evenemen t of the evening, however, was in Cook's next break, when he succeeded in scoring 179, including 44 consecutive spot strokes. After an hour's play Tim. brell was passed, the game standing—Cook, 602 ; Timbrell, 498. After a short interval play was re- sumed, Cook commencing with a break of 86, including 15 spot strokes. From this point Cook's flay was chiefly from the spot, his next noticeable break being 77, which consisted solely of consecutive spot strokes. In the play afterwards Timbrell was particularly un- fortunate, the balls breaking very badly for him. However, he succeeded in making two breaks of 40 and 62 respectively, the latter including 16 off the spot. A break of Cook's made 103, which at once determine i the game' and at the conclusion Cook was 1,001, and Timbrell 675.

To compensate for the disappointment caused by their late arrival, Mr. Brazendale announced that Messrs. Cook and Timbrell had kindly consented to play a return match within a month, and that the ad- mission to the room would lip at a considerably reduced charge. During the evening Mr. Brazendale and his manager, Mr. Bennett, were most attentive to the comfort of the players and the visitors, the arrange- ments for the match also being of a most complete character.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, be- fore Mr. Judge Ffonlkes, a carter, named Yardley, sued two policemen named Ainsworth and McNeill (No, 7 and 11), members of the borough police force for two guineas as compensation for an illegal arrest on the 21st July. The ease for the plaintiff was that one of the defendants charged him with obstructing the road by allowing his horse to stand in Mersey- street. He asked him his name, and subsequently he apprehended him, and took him down to the police station, another officer having preferred a charge against him of furious driving. The plaintiff's attor- ney contended although the plaintiff was convicted of the offence the defendants had no right to arrest him, and walk him through the streets like a felon. For the defence it was contended that the plaintiff was un- known to the police, that he refused to give them his name or to spell it for them, that they did not take him into custody, but that he accompanied the men to the station and asked if "Hunt was in," meaning the chief constable. Although it was argued that the police knew where the man worked, Mr. Nicholson contended that it was necessary to know the plaintiff's private resi- dence, so that there might be a good service of the summons. LECTURE AT BOWDON: OUR SURPLUS POPULATION. The Rev. William. Cunningham delivered a lecture in the Parish Schoolroom, on Friday evening, on political economy. The lecturer, in an address marked by comprehensiveness and detail, pointed out the relation between capital and land. He explained why capital applied to manufacturing was generally more ; remunerative than when applied to the cultivation of • the land. Alderman Machin was of opinion that the fact that so little capital was applied to the land in this country was chiefly due to the law of primogeniture, which seemed to necessitate on the part of the holder of the laud, a provision for the younger branches of his family. This provision practically impoverished the agrioulture of the country. Other causes, doubt- less, operated in the same direction, and prevented the free Sow of capital to land , and it was contended on high authority that under more favourable circum- stances three times the amount of capital might be applied to the land in England, and nearly three times the corn raised for the people here. It was doubtful, in his opinion, whether we could produce an Utopia in England by legislation. There ever arose to neutralise our increased produc- tion the ever-present difficulty of over-population; as the produce of the land increased, it seemed that the people to be fed increased proportionately. While that fact remained, the food diffioulty would remain with it. Increased production caused increased popu- lation, and what was accomplished in onequar ter of a century was overtaken in the next. Emigration, he apprehended, was an equally temporary remedy for the growth of the population. If they supposed that by means of emigration there were only half the people left behind, there would certainly be a diminution of production for some time, but there would be always the same constant tendency for the population to in- crease in numbers, and in 60 or IQO years people would be back in their old state—the half left would have doubled, and this country would be as badly off as ever. There could be no way whatever of counter- acting a constant ever-present tendency by little occa- sional checks here and there—they could not be suffi- cient to keep the one force which was constantly press. lug on us in abeyance, and they were thus brought face to face with the likelihood of a greater amount of want continually increasing in the world. This was the conclu- sion at which Ur. Malthus had arrived, and he asserted that the cause of all the pauperism which existed at his time was to be found in over•population, and in the imprudent marriages which were saade by the labourers of this country. To put it in the short form in which Mr. Malthus gave it, he would say that want could only be temporarily alleviated by increased production or by emigration the constant cause of it lay in over-population. The hindrance to over popu- lation in the future was called a positire check, and one of these positive checks was the ravages of war, another, famine, another, disease ; and another of want, as instanced by the higher rate of mortality amongst children of the lower classes. Population had a tendency to increase faster than the means of subsis- tence, and unless over-population was prevented by prudence in marrying, it would be positively checked by disease and want. Until this was better understood and better recognised he could see no other hope for the suppression of want and misery in this country— all other remedies which might be proposed might after all be mere makeshifts and utterly thrown away.

div.head: AN ALTRINCHAM GROCER AND HIS DOG.
div.p: AN ALTRINCHAM GROCER AND HIS DOG.

Mr. Edward Roose Evans, grocer, of the Downie Altrincham, was summoned at the Altrineham Sessions on Monday, at the instance of Inspector Carter of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, for thet ho, between the 10th October, and the 2nd of November, did unlawfully and cruelly illtreat a dog by neglecting to supply it with sufficient food and water and divers other means." Mr. Hockin prosecuted, and Mr. Atkinson defended. The case for the prosecu- tion was that the defendant, whose shop is opposite Bowdon Station, formerly had business premises on the Downs, which he left some six weeks or two months ago. He removed, it was stated his family, his furni- ture and everything but his dog, which he left chained in the yazd until the visit of the Inspector on the 2nd inst. The dog, according to the prosecution, had been fearfully neglected, and had net been unchained once during that time. There was no shelter, and the dog when found was lying in its own filth, and was in a most disgraceful and pitiable state. The dog,the prosecution said, had not been supplied with eithet .food or water with one or two slight exceptions—once a fortnight or once a week. Inspector Carter found the dog without any shelter, its eyes were bloodshot and the animalbore every appearance, which indicated that it was suffering from the torture of starvation. The piteous howlings of the dog drew the attention of the neighbours to it, and the notice of thelnspector of the Society was directed to the animal. On being charged with the offence the defendant, said that it was very unfortunate, he knew the dog had been neglected, but rnot altogether starved. He left it to his lad to feed, but he, the lad, left last Monday, (this was on Thurs- day.) He had never been to feed it himself during the six weeks it had been there. He was speaking to his wife the previous night about bringing it to the new shop. He had plenty of stuff, and he would see that it was properly fed and looked after. He hoped the Inspector would not report the matter. It was the want of water more than food that the dog was suffer. bog from: If he were summoned it would look bad, because he was summoned for a pony when he was innocent. Inspector Carter, Mr. Thomas Morris, Acting Sergeant Harvey, and Inspector Leigh- ton, were celled for the prosecution. The defence was that the dog had not been neglected as stated by the prosecution, that there was a bag on which the dog could lie, and that it could go into the closet if it wanted shelter. Also that the defendant had given definite orders to his servant to give food to the boys to take to the dog, which the servant swore she had done daily, and the boys said they had taken it, one saying that he went three or four times a week, 1 and another twice a day. The defendant was unaware that the dog had not been fed with the regularity which it might have been, but after arranging with the ser- vants in his employ to feed the dog, he in common with the prosecution could only regret that his order had not been strictly carried out. During the hearing of the case the dog, a medium sized black retriever, was brought into court and bore no signs of the bad treat- ment to which it was said it had been subjected. It was stated by one of the witneeses for the defence that since the 2nd inst. the dog had been fed three times a day, on boiled rabbits potatoes, gravy, and milk. This the prosecution alleged was the result of its good appearance. CELL.

On Monday afternoon Mr. Wortley, deputy coroner, held an inquest at Stockton Heath, on the body of Peter Rush, farm labourer, about 50 years of age, who had died on Saturday morning, under somewhat peculiar circumstances. The deceased was fetching a horte from Bank Quay Station for his master on Friday evening, and it appeared from the evidence of a porter that when he was on the horse it re,red, and the deceased fell backwards, the horse falling upon him. The deceased got up, remarking that he was not much hurt. Rush had had some drink, but was not drunk. Mary Houghton stated that she saw the deceased on Friday night, between seven and eight o'clock, lying on the footpath at Stockton Heath. She went up to him, and helped him up. Deceased, who seemed to be very ill, said that he had a pain in his right side, that his horse had flung him off and kicked him, and that he believed he should_ die. She took him to the London Bridge Inn. Sergeant Bebbington, stationed at Stockton Heath, said that about nine o'clock on Fiilay night last he was asked to go to the London Bridge Inn, which he did, and found the deceased lying in the taproom, be- fore the fire. The deceased appeared to him to be drunk, but could answer any questions that were put to him. Deceased said he had a pain in his head, and wanted to be taken into the adjoining stable, but wit- ness got assistance and took him to the police station at Stockton Heath. They examined the man, as he said he had fallen from a horse, to see if he uad bruises on him, but could only and a scratch on hie hip. He gave the man some tea, and he and P.C. Foden sat up with him till 12 30 a.m., and having covered him up with rugs they left him. In about half an hour after this they gave him some more tea, left him, and spin paid him a visit at ten minutes to two. Deceased was much worse, and he sent P.C. Foden to Warrington for Dr. Gornall. While the officer was away de. ceased vomited, and died at two o'clock, about half an hour before the doctor arrived. Dr. Gornall stated that he saw the deceased shortly after two o'clock on Saturday morning. He was then lying dead in the police cell covered up with rugs. He subsequently made a post-mortem examination Of the body, and the cause of death, in his opinion, was 0, rupture of the bladder, in consequence of the tuariiti falling upon the deceased. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death.

SAD DEATH' OF A SHIP STEWARD
AT RUNCORN.

. On Thuraday an inquest vac held at Runcorn, be. fore Mr. Ridgway, coroner, on the body of Alfred French, 40 years of age, late cook and steward of the brigantine Betty, of London. From the evidence it appeared that the deceased was paid off a week ago at Runcorn, and he then had £3 in money and an order for £lB, payable to him on the Superintendent of St. Catherine's Dock, London. He took lodgings at a private lodging-house kept by a person named Allner, in Percival 's-lane, and during the whole of the time he was in the house he only had one meal He drank is- ordinate quantities of gin, and according to the evi- dence of his landlady, drank as much as four and five half-pint bottles of gin a day. On the Sunday, as she was a Welshwoman, she refused to let him have any drink, and told him the public-houses were shut. He emaibited symptoms of illness, and she said he gave her the £lB order, telling her to keep it for herself. He gradually grew worse, but still refused to see a doctor, and died ou,Dionday night. The coroner remonstrated with the woman for supplying the deceased with so inuc:i drink, and she replied that the man would have it, and he said he was never St to be ashore, he always got drunk. A medical man saw the body after death, and he gave it as his opinion that the deceased had died from starvation, accelerated by excessive drinking. A Russian bailor, and also a Swedish sailor, who shipped with the deceased at North Shields, said although he was a good workman and bore a good character, he frequently got drunk when he had an opportunity ox doing so. The jury returned a verdict of "Death from excessive drinking." A discussion took place relative to the witness Antler being allowed by the authorities to keep a lodging. house without it being registered, and it transpired that the Commissioners had found fault with their officer for visiting private houses, as it was their opinion that only common lodging-houses required registraion. The Coroner thought with the jury, that the house of the witness ought to be registered, and that it was just possible, had the house been open to inspection the deceased would not have been allowed to aye drank himself to death.

DEATH OF THE REV, B. BAGNALL, M.A.

General regret was expressed in Ransom On Mona day at the announcement of the sudden death of the Rev. Samuel Baguall, the incumbent of Weston Point, who for a period of 30 years has been connected with the neighbourhood of Runoorn. The deceased gentlemen, who was 73 years of age, was in his usual health until Saturday last, when he became indisposed through a severe cold, and in consequence was unable to perform his usual Sunday duty. He gradually grew worse, and died early on Monday morning. Mr. Bagnall was one of the oldest clergymen in the diocese of Chester, and was deservedly esteemed. Some time ago the admiration of hie Runcorn friends took a pm. 40.1 shape, and he was presented with a purse of 100 guinea. About three months ago he contracted his second marriage, and he has enjeled remarkably good health until his fatal illness. We understand the in- terment will take place on Saturday afternoon, at the Runcorn Cemetery. The living, which is worth £l6O a year and a house, is in the gift of the River Weaver Trustees.

div.head: WIDNES DIVORCE CASE.
div.p: A WIDNES DIVORCE CASE.

In the Divorce Division of the High Court of Jus- tice, on Friday afternoon, the Right Hon. the Presi- dent had before him the local cause of Barton v. Barton and Harris, which was the petition of the husband for a divorce on the ground of his wife's adultery with the co-respondent. There was no de- fence.

Mr. Bayford stated that the parties were married at Bolton-le-Moors, and the petitioner is now at the CommerCial Hotel, at Rainhill. He formerly resided at Widnes, where he kept the Royal Hotel. The co- respondent is the drill-sergeant to the Rifle Volunteers in the town, and he formerly lodged at the petitioner's' but now lives at the Drill Hall. The petitioner had occasion to complain of his wife being too familiar with Harris and he spoke to her about it, but she told him he had nothing to do with it. tine day the respondent announced her intention of going to see her mother at Belton, and the co-respondent said he was going too. The petitioner, thereupon, protested but to no purpose, and the respondent and the co-respondent met at the house of the former's mother. In consequence of this there was a quarrel, and another one on the return of the parties to Widnes. The petitioner ordered the co- respondent out of the house, but he did not then go. Afterwards the respondent left her husband, and has since lived at the Drill Hall, and there was every rea- son to believe that the co-respondent was the father of twins, of which Mrs. Barton was the mother. The petitioner, George Barton stated that he was married to the respaident on the 10th of August, 1861, at the Roman Catholic Chapel. Afterwards he kept the Royal Hotel, and the co-respondent was a lodger with him, and was the drill instructor to the Rifle Volunteers. He observed familiarities between the co-respondent and his wife. There were quarrels in consequence. Martha Moore, Margaret Wicks, Mr. Husband (the solicitor in the case), and others were examined, and their evidence satisfied the learned judge that the ree- puha and the co-respondent were living at the Drill Hall as man and wife, and a decree nisi with 005 ts, was granted.

THE LIBERAL LEGISLATION OF THE CENTURY: No. T. WITH the declarations of war by France in February, 1798, the first and the peaceful part of Pitt's Administration, says his biographer, Lord Stanhope, ends. It was a period of nine years—the mod prosperous and happy, perhaps, that England ever yet had known. Pitt, though still young, had with consummate skill converted deficiency to surplus' and augmented the revenue while he lessened the taxes. He did this while he was able at the same time to main- tain a firm and resolute tone to foreign powers—as to France and Russia—and the country prospered under a rapid expansion of commerce, and an almost unexampled growth of credit at home. Lord Stanhope wisely shows that the benefit of these mea- sures was by no means limited to the period thus described, "since it was mainly the sap and strength imparted by them which enabled the nation to sustain and finally triumph ovei the perils of the conflict that ensued." This is quite true. It was the reversal of this policy—a necessity, perhaps, if war was to be carried on—which im- poverished England for half a century: it was the return to this system by Peel and Gladstone, backed by the repeal of the corn- law, which has doubled our population, and caused trade to increase "by leaps and bounds." It is somewhat difficult for us to fairly judge the Ministry in their action towards France. England's policy was to have been neutral. Had she remained so, it is pro- bable we should have avoided a long and costly war with France, that we should have been spared some painful humiliation in diplomacy as well as in arms, and that we should have escaped the rupture with America in 1812. There is no doubt that we should have been prosperous at home, that the darkest pages in the political his- tory of this century would never have been written, that our progress in trade and com- merce would have been unexampled, and that instead of our liberties :having been re- duced, and subjected to the penalties arising from the falsehoods of spies and informers, they would much earlier "have broadened down from precedent to precedent" than they did. We were, unhappily, burdened with treaties, and we had that dreadful "balance of power" ever before us. It is doubtful whether Pitt was ever eager for the war: his colleagues were much more ;eager than he; and at the close of the Reign of Terror in 1798, Pitt was most anxious to enter into negociations with the French Government. Lord Malmesbury was sent with large powers to treat, but he had to return from a fruit- less errand. Again in 1797 fresh overtures were made, but with no better result. Our cheeks burn as we now read of the humilia- tions our Ambassador was subjected to, and the insults he, or rather England through him, had to endure. Barras, representing the Directory, made an overture for peace on.the terms proposed by the British Govern- ment, with the surrender of Ceylon, and the dotation of two millions sterling to himself and his friends of the Directory. Pitt actu- ally obtained the consent of the King and the members of the Cabinet to entertain this proposal, abating the demand to £450,000. "The very fact that Pitt did not immediately reject such an overture," says ta sn,t- -v drgai opinion has attributed to him, he was for peace at any price." The war was entered upon in consequence of a treaty made in 1788 by England and France, to guarantee to Holland the exclusive navigation of the Scheldt and Meuse. France broke her agreement, and instructed her general in Flanders to employ the moans at his dis- posal for the -opening of the Dutch waters. But an equally strong reason for going to war was that the Tory party of the day so cordially detested the Republican ideas of the French, they were determined to put them down if possible. It was for this reason they joined with Austria, Prussia, and Holland in attacking the armies of the Republic: it was for this that subscriptions were raised, volunteers enrolled, army corps formed, and the nation went mad for glory. Nowhere was this fever hotter than at Manchester, and nowhere were the friends of peace subjected to greater indignities. They said "We have nothing to do with the government of France or of any other.nation, let the people settle that themselves." But they were not listened to. The people were set against "Jacobonisto." ; armies were sent abroad to be beaten; allies—Prussia, Austria, Holland ' —each sought their own interests; and we , were left to make the ignominious offers,' already alluded to. Our only redeeming efforts were those of the navy, and foolish and wicked as the war was, England hasi cause to be proud of the prowess of her sailors, Meanwhile therCwas trouble at home. The war, and the bad harvest trebled the price of food, work was scarce, want stalked at large. Even our navy, elated with victory, the source of our pride, mutinied at I Chatham and at the Nore, and large con- cessions had to be made. Our public men were silenced, and like Thomas Walker were arrested for treason, and put upon their trial. Our penal code was atrociously cruel and wicked. Persons who broke into a dwelling-house, or stole from it, or from a shop, property of the value of five shillings, were hanged. A painful story illustrative of this, is told of a poor woman whose hus- band was seized by the press.gang on his return from work. In vain did the wife, , unconscious of what had happened, wait for , her good man's return. The agony of sus- pense, and of supposed desertion had to be increased by her anxiety for food for herself and children. She could not get work, so one by one the household treasures gathered together after much toil, had to be sold. At last everything was gone. There was not even the chilling refuge of the Workhouse to fly to. In despair she stole a pocket- handkerchief from a shop, was caught, con- victed, and hanged. It is said that this shameful case spurred on Sir Samuel Romilly till he got the law reduced to a more merciful condition. Meanwhile people w ere ashamed of the wholesale executions, and criminals were sent to Norfolk Island or Botany Bay. It is said that between the years 1787 and 1792, five thousand convicts were transported to these stations. A writer states that in the first years of the colony, these wretched creatures were literally slaves, employed in clearing woods to gain a space for cultivation, half-starved, with no hope of escape, with the sea before them, and a boundless waste behind. Southey thus depicts the hopeless condition of one, whose worst am possibly was, that she had stolen some trilling article to save herself from starvation, urged to it by the high prices, the reduced wages, and the want of work caused by a foolish war. iffinother direction. It is quite true that at first public opinion was in favour of the war. The bulk of the aristocracy liked it because it was a war more of opinion than of any defined object; it was to suppress democracy, it raised the status of the gentry who became officers of fencibles, volunteers, or militia. It increased the value of land, and raised rents. The farmers liked it because when competition was removed they were enriched. The people liked it for its show, its pride and pomp, and the pro- mise of glory. But when glory was turned into shame, when our land forces were beaten, when food was trebled in value and became scarce, when the Govern- ment shrank from public opinion, and sup- pressed free discussion and prosecuted the press—then there arose men who for a while had to suffer, but who secured to us at last the inestimable blessings of liberty of speech and thought. Thomas Walker, at Man- chester; Muir and Palmer, in Scotland; Hardy, Home Tooke, and others in London had asserted, that freedom in the governed to complain of wrongs, and readiness in rulers to redress them, constitute the ideal of a free state. "Philosophers and statesmnn of all ages "says Sir Erskine May, "have asserted the claims of liberty of opinion. But the very causes which have filled enlightened thinkers with admiration for this liberty, have provoked the intolerance of rulers. It was nobly said by Erskine, that other liberties are held under governments, but the liberty of opinion keeps governments themselves in due subj ection to their duties. This has produced the martyrdom of truth in every age; and the world has only been purged from ignorance with the innocent blood of those who have enlightened it.' The church has persecuted freedom of thought in religion, the State has repressed it in politics. Everywhere authority has resented discus- sion, as hostile to its own sovereign rights. Hence, in states otherwise free, liberty of opinion has been the last political privilege which the people have acquired." Years after these and other brave men had suffered, after the Courier (not that at Manchester!) proprietors, who had written against the Emperor of Russia, had been told by the Bench that public writers were to be punished, not for their guilt, but from fear of the displeasure of foreign powers. Sheridan, in reviewing the past, could justly Bay—" Give me but the liberty of the press, and I will give the minister a venal House of Peers, I will give him a corrupt and servile House of Commons, I will give him the full swing of the patronage of office, I will give him the whole host of ministerial influence, I will give him all the power that place can confer upon him to purchase submission, and averawe resistance; and yet, armed with the liberty of the press, I will go forth to meet him undismayed, I will attack the mighty fabric he has reared, with that mightier engine, I will shake down from its height, corruption, and lay it beneath the ruins of the abuses it was meant to shelter." It is to the Liberal legislation of the century we owe these blessings.

The appointment of Lord Salisbury as the representative of England at the forth- coming Conference of the Great Powers on Eastern Affairs, continues to divide the public interest with the strange speech of the Prime Minister at the Guildhall, in which he may be said, metaphorically, to have shaken his fist in the face of Russia. Foreign journals interpret Lord Beacons- field's declaration variously, but the opinion generally prevails that the time is badly chosen for uttering threatening language when the Conference is about to enter on its mission of conciliation and peace.

Amongst journals at home the Times observes that what Lord Beaconsfield said at the Lord Mayor's ban- quet will be as gravely interpreted as if he had never before disconcerted slow-witted commentators on his paradoxical sentences. He had something substantial te say, but enveloped it in a cloud of grandiloquent mystery. To Lord Beaconsfield's bellicose grand eloquence and my story, the Czar lost no time in replying, on the fore- noon ofthe 10th, Addressing the Communal Council of Moscow, the Emperor of All the Russians said, "Should I see that we cannot obtain such guarantees as are necessary from the Porte, I am lir ai!), determined to act independently, and I am convinced that in this Case the whole of Russia will respond to my summons. May God help us to carry out our sacred mission!" One can hardly wonder that these warlike speeches greatly influenced transactions on the Stock Exchange. All the principal securities declined, more particularly consols, railway shares, and foreign stocks. It was fully recagnised on the Stock Exchange that the Prime Minister is bent on maintaining the integrity of the Ottoman Empire at all hazards, and that he is likely to drag his colleagues in the Cabinet along with him in his perilous course.

Mr. I:owe—amongst English politicians—has th is week spoken decisively on the Eastern_ question, and of the Premier's deploratle braggadocia. He said he neYer remembered so strong and unanimous an ex- pression of opinion as was evinced when the news arrived of the Bulgarian atrocities. Her Majesty's Government had refused to take any adequate notice of that opinion. Earl Beaconsfield had taken credit for the consistency of the Government in maintaining Turkish integrity, the atrocities inflicted upon the Christians notwithstanding. Mr. Lowe lamented the absence of the Liberals from power when there was an Imminent possibility of England being engaged in a war Of which every Englishman ought to be ashamed. He characterised Lord Beaconsfield's Guildhall boast- ing as unnecessary and deplorable. Russia had answered, "If you are ready for war so am I, and I era quite prepared to meet you." Mr. Lswe thought the Conference could lead to no good, and that the peace of Europe was in imminent jeopardy. As a practical commentory on his own answer to the Guildhall defiance, it was stated on Wednesday, that orders have been given by the Czar for the mobilisation of part of the Russian army. Prince Gortschakoff, in a circular to the Russian representatives abroad, ex- plaining the measure, says that the Emperor does not desire war, and will, if possible, avoid it. He is, how- ever, determined th at the principles of justice which have been recognised as necessary by the whole of Europe shall be carried out in Turkey under efficient guarantees. Intelligenee received in &main, from St. Petersburg, states that the Russian army is ready to take the field.

What manner of Empire it is which this country seems pledged by its Prime Minister to support with incalculable blood and treasure the following extra° from the Daily IVien of Wednesday will enable the country to judge. The Daily NetoB says !—" We publish this morning a letter from our Special Com, missicner in Bulgaria giving many illustrations of the corruption and injustice of Turkish rule there. Our Commissioner maintains that no kind of diplomatic fiction or jugglery can bolster up that rule much longer. Its end, he says, is near and inevitable: it is pataoug aw acao LCusdo u& uppUblllg circumstances than by the ignorance, imbecility, and barbarism of those who administer it. The Consuls adopt this view, and even Mr. Baring has expressed a very decided opinion in the same sense. The Turks are net, as is supposed, doing atything to restore law and order to the province. To the reign of terror has succeeded a period of lawlessness and violence which is full of threats for the future. In a word the country Is drifting into a state of anarchy and confusion, from which, our Commissioner says, it can only be rcslued by a foreign intervention."

Sir George Campbell, KR, writing to his consti- tuents from Turkey, confirms the reports which have been published respecting the atrocities in Bulga- ria. In Batak there are not now nearly so many people as Mr. Baring reported to have been left alive. Sir George expresses a hope that our Government will be firm and determined in their negotiations with Tur- key, and that in their endeavours to do right they will be backed up by the country.
